food.text: In 17th-century Egypt, food culture reflected a stark divide between urban elites and rural peasants. What people ate depended heavily on where they lived and how wealthy they were.
Peasants in 17th-century Egypt relied on simple staples such as ful medames, stewed fava beans, along with molokheya, lentils and barley bread. These meals were often garnished with onions.

Urban cuisine in 17th-century Egypt, particularly among the Ottoman-influenced elites, featured refined versions of peasant dishes. Cooks incorporated butter, meats and elaborate seasonings to raise them above everyday village fare.
Peasant diets included keshk, a fermented grain and dairy food, and mish, a fermented cheese. Fermentation turned grain and dairy into staples the peasants could rely on.
Fish was common in 17th-century Egypt, particularly mullet and seabream, prepared in stews or served with keshk. Fesikh, salt-cured fish, remained a delicacy.
Poultry and meat were rare in peasant diets but abundant in city kitchens. Urban dishes included stuffed pigeons and rich stews.

Despite the divide between rich and poor, many core ingredients stayed central to Egyptian cooking in the 17th century. Fava beans, molokheya and preserved dairy appeared across both peasant and elite tables.

art.text: The Mamluk Sultanate ruled Egypt from 1250 to 1517, when it was conquered by the Ottoman Empire. Even after that conquest, the traditional Mamluk building style continued to be used in Cairo. It was often combined to some degree with Ottoman architectural elements.

Starting in the mid-18th century, icon painting enjoyed a revival in Egypt and became popular once again. Coptic icons are more concerned with religious truth and beauty than with realism, depth, or perspective. Their figures are shown frontally, looking straight at the viewer.

The building of Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral in Azbakeya, Cairo, in the late eighteenth century marked the beginning of a revival of Coptic architecture. It came after long restrictions on church building under the Ottomans.

One of the most famous icon painters of the mid-18th-century revival was Yuhanna al-Armani. His works were noted for more developed techniques and novel construction. For example, he used a set of icons to tell a single story.

In the eighteenth century, European architectural styles began to influence Coptic churches. This added to a tradition that over two thousand years had already absorbed native Egyptian, Greco-Roman, Byzantine and Western European styles.

French forces arrived in the Campaign in Egypt and Syria in 1798 and saw Egypt's ancient monuments and images. As a result, Westerners began to study Egyptian beliefs firsthand, and Egyptian religious motifs were adopted into Western art.

art.text: Regulations put in place by the Ottomans prevented the building of new churches in Egypt. These restrictions lasted more than three hundred years, and were eased only progressively by later governments. Only then could many churches be rebuilt and new ones built.

war.text: The Ottomans conquered Mamluk Egypt in 1517 and ruled it as a province, or eyalet, of their empire. Egypt proved a difficult province for the sultans to control, partly because of the continuing power of the Mamluks, the military caste who had ruled the country for centuries.
Egypt stayed semi-autonomous under the Mamluks for nearly three centuries of Ottoman rule. That ended only when Napoleon Bonaparte's French forces invaded in 1798.

In 1707 the pasha of the time sowed enmity between two Mameluke factions, the Qasimites and the Fiqarites. A fight between them outside Cairo lasted eighty days, and at the end of it Qasim Iywaz, who led the Qasimites, was killed. His office of shaykh al-balad went to his son Ismail.

In 1724 Ismail was assassinated through the machinations of the pasha, and Shirkas Bey of the opposing faction was elevated to the office of Sheikh al-Balad in his place. Dhu-'l-Fiqar, one of his own faction, soon drove him from his post and he fled to Upper Egypt. After a short time Shirkas Bey returned at the head of an army, and in the last of the ensuing battles he met his end by drowning.

Dhu-'l-Fiqar, who had driven Shirkas Bey from office, was himself assassinated in 1730. His place was filled by Othman Bey, who had served as his general in the war against Shirkas Bey. In 1743 Othman Bey was forced to flee Egypt by the intrigues of two adventurers, Ibrahim and Ridwan Bey, who once their scheme had succeeded began a massacre of beys and others thought to be opposed to them.

literature.text: The printing press first came to Egypt with Napoleon's campaign in 1798, at the very end of the Early Modern era. It would go on to radically change Egypt's literary output.
The Rosetta Stone was discovered on July 15, 1799, in the port town of Rosetta, Egypt. It is a tablet written in ancient Greek, Egyptian Demotic script and Egyptian hieroglyphs.

Athanasius Kircher (1601-1680) was the first person in Europe to realize that Coptic was a direct linguistic descendant of ancient Egyptian. This was an important step toward understanding Egypt's ancient writing.
In his Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Athanasius Kircher made the first concerted European effort to interpret the meaning of Egyptian hieroglyphs. His attempt was based on symbolic inferences.

The Rosetta Stone's three scripts included ancient Greek, a well-known language. That gave linguists the ability to decipher the mysterious Egyptian hieroglyphic language, opening hundreds of texts and inscriptions that had been indecipherable.

science.text: Athanasius Kircher (1601–1680) was the first in Europe to realize that Coptic was a direct linguistic descendant of ancient Egyptian. In his Oedipus Aegyptiacus he made the first concerted European effort to interpret the meaning of Egyptian hieroglyphs, though it rested on symbolic inferences.

The question of the race of the ancient Egyptians was raised as a product of the early racial concepts of the 18th and 19th centuries. These ideas were linked to models of racial hierarchy based primarily on craniometry and anthropometry. Georges Cuvier, the leading French scientist of the 18th century, considered the Egyptians to be Caucasian.

The Ancient Egyptian language is classified into six major chronological divisions, and the last of them is Coptic. Coptic was used as a working language until the 18th century CE. It is still used today as a liturgical language by Egyptian Copts.

The French scholar Volney visited Egypt between 1783 and 1785. His travel notes describe the Sphinx as "typically negro in all its features". A similar early description came from Vivant Denon, who called the Sphinx's character "African" with thick lips.

politics.text: In the 16th century Nubia was partitioned. The northern half was conquered by the Ottoman Empire and the southern half by the Sennar sultanate. This followed the decline of the Christian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia, which had endured for roughly a millennium.
The Mamluk Sultanate was ruled from Cairo by a military caste of mamluks, freed slave soldiers, headed by a sultan. The Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1517, ending Mamluk rule.

After the Ottomans conquered Mamluk Egypt in 1517, they ruled it as a province, or eyalet. Egypt proved difficult for the sultans to control because the Mamluks stayed powerful. It remained semi-autonomous under them until Napoleon Bonaparte's French forces invaded in 1798.

The Funj Sultanate was established in 1504 by Sultan Amara Dunqas, a convert to Islam who founded its capital Sennar on the Blue Nile. It succeeded the medieval Nubian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia. It reached its peak in the late 17th century.

Qansuh al-Ghuri, the last effective Mamluk sultan, reigned from 1501 to 1516. His reign was known for heavy-handed fiscal policies, including taxation and extortion that provoked sometimes violent protests, as well as attempted military reforms and confrontations with the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean. In 1516, at the Battle of Marj Dabiq, the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeated his army after Khayr Bak betrayed him mid-battle, and in the chaos al-Ghuri was killed.

By the 18th century, the Ottoman pasha mattered less than the Mamluk beys. Two offices held by Mamluks, Shaykh al-Balad and Amir al-hajj, represented the real headship of the community. The article says how this came about is obscure, because good chronicles for the Turkish period are lacking.

The decline of Makuria and Alodia led to the partition of Nubia in the 16th century. The northern half was conquered by the Ottoman Empire and the southern half by the Sennar sultanate. The change was followed by a rapid process of Islamization and partial Arabization of the Nubian people.

By the 18th century the importance of the Ottoman pasha in Egypt was superseded by that of the Mameluk beys. Two offices, Shaykh al-Balad and Amir al-hajj, were held by Mamluks and represented the real headship of the community.

Some Christian Nubian refugees eventually established the Kingdom of Fazughli after the last Nubian kingdom collapsed around 1504. It survived for well over a century before the Funj conquered it in 1685.

Qaitbay's death on 8 August 1496 began several years of instability in Egypt. After several brief reigns by other candidates, Qansuh al-Ghuri was placed on the throne in 1501. He appointed his nephew Tuman Bay as dawadar and his second in command.

In 1707 the shaykh al-balad Qasim Iywaz headed one of two Mameluke factions, the Qasimites and the Fiqarites, whose enmity the pasha of the time had sown. The factions fought for eighty days outside Cairo. Qasim Iywaz was killed, and his office passed to his son Ismail.

Ismail held the office of shaykh al-balad for 16 years while the pashas were constantly being changed, and he reconciled the two Mameluke factions. In 1724 he was assassinated through the machinations of the pasha. Shirkas Bey, of the opposing faction, was elevated in his place.

In 1743/1744 Sultan Badi of Sennar had his vizier executed and took power, supported by his slave army. He purged the previous ruling clan, stripped the nobility of their land and empowered clients from the western and southern periphery instead, and grew increasingly unpopular for his repressive measures. Muhammad Abu Likaylik, a Hamaj, was convinced by disaffected Funj noblemen to march on the capital; a council at Alays deposed Badi, and Abu Likaylik entered Sennar on 27 March 1762, beginning the Hamaj Regency, in which the Funj monarchs became puppets. Badi fled to Ethiopia but was murdered in 1763.

Shirkas Bey was soon driven from his post by Dhu-'l-Fiqar, one of his own faction, and fled to Upper Egypt. He returned at the head of an army and drowned in the last of the ensuing battles. Dhu-'l-Fiqar was himself assassinated in 1730, and his general Othman Bey took his place.

In 1711 an event chroniclers called the "Great Sedition" occurred in Ottoman Egypt. A religious fanatic preacher publicly denounced praying at the graves of Sufi saints, sparking a religious movement. It was not crushed until 1714.

The Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Qansuh al-Ghawri left Cairo on 18 May 1516 with a large army that was well equipped in all respects but artillery. Accompanying him were 5,000 of his own royal Mamluks, fifteen high-ranking emirs, and even the Abbasid caliph Al-Mutawakkil III.

philosophy.text: The Mamluks were a military caste originally formed of enslaved soldiers under Ayyubid rule. They eventually seized power and governed Egypt until the Ottoman conquest in 1517. Through these centuries Sunni Islam became entrenched as the dominant religious identity, and Al-Azhar emerged as a preeminent center of Sunni Islamic learning.

Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani (1492/3–1565) was an Egyptian jurist, historian, mystic and theologian. He is regarded as "one of the last original thinkers in Islam." He founded an Egyptian Sufi order named after him.

Murtada al-Zabidi (1732–1790) was an Indian Sunni polymath who settled in Cairo. He was a Hanafi scholar, mystic and theologian, and was considered one of the leading intellectuals of the 18th century.

Al-Sha'rani studied all four Sunni schools of Islamic jurisprudence. This places him among the few Islamic scholars in history to master all four madhabs. His highest fame came through the Shafi'i school.

Al-Sha'rani stood for a traditional, moderately ascetic, non-political and orthodox strain of Egyptian Sufism. Shadhili ethics and literature influenced him, but he did not join that tariqa because he found it too aristocratic.

Murtada al-Zabidi's fame spread far beyond Egypt. Rulers from the Hejaz, India, Yemen, the Levant, Iraq, Morocco, Turkey, Sudan and Algiers corresponded with him. Some people in Western Africa believed their Hajj was incomplete if they did not plan to see him.

The Funj Sultanate encouraged the spread of Islam by inviting Sufi holymen to its lands, which also accelerated Arabization and the formation of the modern Sudanese Arab tribes. Yet the Funj's own embrace of Islam was only nominal. Their Sultan was a divine king who could be executed if judged wanting. Among the populace pork and beer were staple foods, and a death was mourned with "communal dancing, self-mutilation and rolling in the ashes of the feast-fire". In some regions the elderly, crippled and others seen as a burden were expected to ask to be buried alive or otherwise disposed of.

Before the French campaign under Napoleon Bonaparte, religious functionaries handled almost all of Egypt's educational, legal, public health and social welfare issues. Under the Ottoman Empire, the public and political roles of the ulama, the Muslim religious scholars, were reinforced.

By the seventeenth century, western Sudan had come under the Islamic rule of the Sultanate of Darfur. Like the Funj Sultanate, it was an indigenous state, so Islam in the region was carried by local rulers.

Al-Sha'rani belonged socially to the Badawiyya, the Sufi order of Ahmad al-Badawi, whom he admired. Yet he vehemently opposed that order and others like it for their excesses, their disdain for Sharia law and their lack of respect for the ulama.

Al-Sha'rani died on 5 December 1565 and was buried in the Zawiya created for him. His son 'Abd al-Rahim succeeded him as its leader. His order gradually declined after his death, though it remained active until the 19th century.

Murtada al-Zabidi wrote Alfiyyah as-Sanad, "A Thousand Liner on Chains of Authentication" in hadith. It is a poem of more than 1500 lines, and he also wrote an explanation of it. He died in Cairo during an epidemic of plague in 1790.
The last Nubian kingdom collapsed around 1504, and Christian Nubian refugees eventually established the Kingdom of Fazughli. It survived as a Christian remnant until the Funj conquered it in 1685.
Al-Sha'rani disparaged the Khalwati order, which was once prominent among Turkish soldiers. He claimed it encouraged hallucinations rather than genuine religious experience.
Al-Sha'rani was introduced into 26 tariqas, but this appears to have been merely ceremonial or done to earn barakah. He never expressed his own tariqa affiliation.

culture.text: After the Christian kingdoms of Nubia fell in the sixteenth century, Islam spread to the region peacefully. Muslim Kenzi preachers and merchants intermarried with the Christian Danagla, and this slowly changed the religion of the Nile valley.

The French Campaign in Egypt and Syria in 1798 greatly increased the influence of ancient Egyptian religion on modern societies. Seeing the monuments and images, Westerners began to study Egyptian beliefs firsthand. Egyptian religious motifs were then adopted into Western art.

In 1504 the native Funj Sultanate became the first Muslim polity established in the Nubian region. It attracted Sufi scholars and religious teachers from Egypt and the Hejaz, which linked Sudan's religious life to the wider Islamic world.

Lower Nubia had become more Arabized and Islamicized and was de facto independent as the state of al-Maris. Most of it was formally annexed by Egypt during the Ottoman conquest of 1517, and it has remained part of Egypt since then.

Islamic religious brotherhoods, or Sufi orders, first came to Sudan in the sixteenth century and became significant in the eighteenth. Sufism seeks a closer personal relationship with God through special spiritual disciplines. The orders made Islam's deepest and longest lasting impact in Sudan.

The influx of Arabs and Nubians to Egypt and Sudan contributed to the suppression of Nubian identity after the last Nubian kingdom collapsed around 1504. Even so, Nubians are still marked out by their distinctive dress, dances, traditions and music.

The Sufi exercise known as dhikr involves reciting prayers and Qur'an passages and repeating the names of God while performing physical movements. Singing and dancing may be introduced. It lasts much longer than daily prayer and often ends in a state of ecstatic abandon.

David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra recorded around 1525 that people in Egypt eat cannabis leaves raw and are inebriated by them, and that they say it makes one happy. He also noted that in some places the plant was used like linen to make garments.
